topStories.headline: Chan Concedes to Wiener, Leaving the Richmond's Supervisor Seat in Limbo
topStories.dek: Supervisor Connie Chan's loss in the congressional race means District 1 — which covers the Richmond and neighboring west-side neighborhoods — will need a new representative on the Board of Supervisors.
topStories.body:
Connie Chan, who has represented District 1 on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors since 2021, conceded her congressional race to state Sen. Scott Wiener on Wednesday, November 4, saying she no longer saw a path to victory. Wiener led by roughly 11 percentage points with about 62 percent of votes counted at the time Chan called him to concede, and final tallies from the Department of Elections — which are not certified until December 3 — are expected to widen the gap further.

Wiener's victory is historic: it marks the first time in nearly four decades that someone other than Nancy Pelosi will represent California's 11th Congressional District, which covers most of San Francisco. Pelosi had endorsed Chan and fundraised heavily for her, but Wiener and his allies outspent Chan's campaign by roughly three to one.

For the Richmond, the more immediate consequence is the vacancy Chan's departure will create on the Board of Supervisors. District 1 encompasses the Inner and Outer Richmond, Sea Cliff, and parts of the northwest side. Under the City Charter, Mayor Daniel Lurie will appoint a replacement to serve until the next election. No appointment timeline has been announced as of press time.

Chan, in her concession statement, said she would continue organizing around affordability, immigrant rights, and workers' issues. Wiener said he is ready to bring housing, transit, and health care priorities to Washington.

topStories.headline: Voters Kill Prop G Citywide, but the Richmond Wanted Cars Back on the Great Highway
topStories.dek: San Francisco rejected the third ballot measure in six years over the Great Highway by a wide margin — yet precinct maps show the Richmond and other west-side neighborhoods voted the other way.
topStories.body:
San Francisco voters on November 3 defeated Proposition G, which would have reopened the Upper Great Highway to car traffic on weekdays while keeping it as a pedestrian park on weekends. With roughly 75 percent of ballots counted as of Thursday, the No side held a commanding 64 percent to 36 percent lead, and the measure's opponents declared victory.

Prop G sought to reverse Proposition K, the November 2024 measure that permanently closed the two-mile coastal road to cars and established what is now called Sunset Dunes Park along Ocean Beach. The citizen's initiative got onto this year's ballot after a similar effort by District 4 Supervisor Alan Wong to place a comparable measure on the June primary ballot fell short.

For Richmond residents, the result arrives with a geographic asterisk. A precinct-by-precinct analysis published by the San Francisco Chronicle found that much of the Richmond, Sunset, and Parkside neighborhoods voted in favor of Prop G — a continuation of the same west-side-versus-east-side divide that has defined the Great Highway debate for six years. Supporters in the area have consistently argued that the road closure pushes cut-through traffic onto Geary, Fulton, and other neighborhood arteries.

The Department of Elections will not issue certified results until December 3, but the margin is considered insurmountable. It is the third consecutive time city voters have resolved — for or against cars on that stretch of coastline — only to relitigate the question at the next election cycle.

topStories.headline: Presidio Trust Opens Its Boardroom to the Public on November 12 — First Meeting Since Trump Fired the Full Board
topStories.dek: The Presidio Trust holds its fall public board meeting at the Officers' Club on November 12, the first such gathering since the entire Biden-appointed board was dismissed in April.
topStories.body:
The Presidio Trust will host its fall Public Board of Directors Meeting on Thursday, November 12, from 6 to 8 p.m. at the Presidio Officers' Club, 50 Moraga Avenue. The meeting is open to the public and registration is encouraged to help the Trust plan for seating.

The agenda includes a Board Chair report, a fiscal year 2026 year-in-review and preview of fiscal year 2027 priorities, updates from the National Park Service and the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy, and an open public comment period on any matter under the Trust's jurisdiction.

The meeting takes place against an unsettled political backdrop for the park's governing body. In April, President Trump sent termination letters to all six members of the Trust's board, all of whom had been appointed by former President Biden. The Trust confirmed the firings at the time and said it was waiting for new appointees. As of this week, the composition of the reconstituted board has not been publicly announced, making this public meeting an opportunity for Presidio neighbors and park users to hear directly from whoever is now seated.

The Presidio Trust manages the 1,500-acre former military base as a self-sustaining unit of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, funding operations through leases on homes and commercial spaces within the park.

moreNews.headline: El Mansour on Clement Street Served as a Polling Place on Election Day
moreNews.body: The Inner Richmond's El Mansour restaurant — known for its Moroccan cuisine and belly dancing shows on weekend evenings — doubled as one of San Francisco's more aromatic polling stations on November 3. Mission Local reported voters casting ballots there throughout the day as results in the congressional and supervisor races came in.

moreNews.headline: Three Incumbent Supervisors — Including Richmond-Adjacent District 2 — Win Re-Election Easily
moreNews.body: Preliminary results from the November 3 election show District 2 Supervisor Stephen Sherrill, whose district borders Sea Cliff and the northern Richmond along the waterfront, on track to win re-election, along with District 4's Alan Wong and District 6's Matt Dorsey. The San Francisco Department of Elections had counted 206,320 ballots as of the November 4 update; certified results are not expected until December 3.

restaurants.name: Hokkaido Sashimi Marketplace
